name: Drometrizole trisiloxane
lead: Drometrizole trisiloxane (INCI name; sold by L'Oreal as Mexoryl XL, also called silatrizole) is a lipophilic benzotriazole-derived organic ultraviolet filter used in sunscreens and daily-wear skincare products [1]. It is described as a broad-spectrum absorber with peaks near 303 nm (UVB) and 344 nm (UVA) and is frequently formulated together with ecamsule (Mexoryl SX) [1][2].

It is approved for sunscreens in the European Union, Canada, Australia, Japan and other countries but is not approved in the United States [1]. In appearance-focused skincare it is mentioned in discussions of photoprotection against pigmentation and photoaging; published work is mostly formulation, photoprotection and contact-allergy research rather than trials of cosmetic outcomes.

paras: The compound is a benzotriazole derivative bearing a siloxane group, with a molar mass of about 502 g/mol [1]. Reviews of sunscreen filters list it alongside terephthalylidene dicamphor sulfonic acid (Mexoryl SX) and methylene bis-benzotriazolyl tetramethylbutylphenol among the newer photostable filters [3].

It is used in sunscreen and daily skincare formulations to broaden UVA and UVB coverage [1][3]. Analytical chemistry papers include it among the UV filters monitored in commercial suncare products [4]. A study of sunscreens and skin pigmentation reported protection against UV-induced pigmentation by products containing Mexoryl filters [5].

Case reports describe allergic contact dermatitis to drometrizole trisiloxane in a sunscreen, with concomitant sensitivities to other sunscreen ingredients [6], and in a woman later diagnosed with frontal fibrosing alopecia [7]. A multicentre European photopatch study registered 1,000 participants to examine photocontact dermatitis from UV filters [8].

No clinical trial dedicated to drometrizole trisiloxane alone as a cosmetic ingredient was found. Studies that included products containing it examined photoprotection in lupus erythematosus patients under photoprovocation testing [9], prevention of UV-induced pigmentation [5], and a registered trial of UV and UV-visible photoprotection in melasma [10]. Because these used finished sunscreens, effects cannot be attributed to this filter alone.

It is permitted in the EU, Canada, Australia and Japan, and is not approved in the United States [1]. A 2025 review argued that newer filters not available in the US could improve public health if regulations were modernized [11].

card.summary: Photostable L'Oreal UVA/UVB sunscreen filter (Mexoryl XL), approved in the EU and elsewhere but not in the US.
card.note: Not an FDA-approved US sunscreen active; rare contact-allergy case reports.

quick.overview:
Drometrizole trisiloxane, sold as Mexoryl XL, is an organic UV filter that absorbs both UVB and UVA light. It is commonly paired with ecamsule (Mexoryl SX) in sunscreens.

It is approved in the EU, Canada, Australia and Japan but not in the United States. Evidence on it comes mainly from formulation and photoprotection studies of finished products.
quick.mechanism: It absorbs ultraviolet radiation, with peaks around 303 nm and 344 nm, and converts it to less harmful energy within the sunscreen film.
quick.risks: Case reports describe allergic contact dermatitis to it. It is not an approved US sunscreen active, so US availability depends on products using other filters.
